titre: Hobbes (1651): The “War of Every Man Against Every Man” Is Not a Fight
accroche: In Leviathan, the war of all against all means the absence of a common power, not a continuous massacre.
contenu_vulgarise:
“The war of every man against every man” is how Thomas Hobbes is often summed up, along with the idea that man is a wolf to man. In *Leviathan* (1651), in chapter XIII, the formula is more precise and more limited.

## War as a Disposition

Hobbes writes that, as long as men live without a common power to keep them all in awe, they are in that condition called war, “and a war of every man against every man.” But he immediately adds that war “does not consist only in battle”: it lies in a span of time in which the will to fight is known. He compares it to the weather: foul weather is not just a shower or two, it is an inclination that lasts for several days. War is likewise a known disposition to fight, as long as there is no assurance to the contrary, and “all other time is peace.”

## Proof From Everyday Life

For anyone who doubts this, Hobbes invites a look at oneself: we arm ourselves when we travel, we lock our doors at night, we lock our chests in our own house, and we do so while knowing that there are laws and armed public officers to avenge wrongs. This accuses mankind by its actions, he says, as much as he accuses it by his words. But he adds that neither accuses the nature of man: desires and passions are not in themselves a sin, and become one only when a law forbids them, a law that cannot be made without agreeing on the person who will make it.

## What He Does Not Say

He himself writes that such a condition was “never generally so, over all the world.” Yet he sees it at work in “many places”: among peoples of America whom he judges to be without government, in a situation of civil war, and between sovereigns, “in the posture of gladiators,” weapons pointed. The argument is therefore a piece of reasoning about what happens when the common power is missing, supported by examples he holds to be real, not a description of a universal past. As for the wolf, it comes from Plautus, whom Hobbes cites in 1642 in the dedicatory epistle of *De Cive* alongside its opposite: man is a god to man when citizens are compared with one another, a wolf when cities are compared.

There remains the question his armed traveler leaves open: how much security does it take to stop locking one's door?

repere.texte: Hobbes writes that life without a common power is “solitary, poore, nasty, brutish, and short”.
repere.source: Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), ch. XIII, Project Gutenberg

carte.punch: For Hobbes, the war of all against all is a climate, not a continuous battle.
carte.idee: In Leviathan (1651), Hobbes compares war to foul weather: it lies in a known disposition to fight, as long as no common power reassures anyone. He writes that this condition was never general.

quiz.question: According to Leviathan, what does the “war of every man against every man” consist of?
choix: A permanent, real fight among all men since the origin of humanity
A natural wickedness of man, which he regards as a sin in itself
A known disposition to fight, as long as no common power assures anyone of the contrary
A war limited to sovereigns alone, with individuals always remaining at peace
quiz.explication: Hobbes compares war to foul weather: a lasting inclination, not endless battles. He says this condition was never general, and that the passions are not a sin in themselves.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What everyday example does Hobbes give to support his argument?
choix: Neighbors fight duels to defend their honor
People lock their chests at home, even though laws and officers exist
People file lawsuits over a debt unpaid for years
People riot in the cities when bread runs short
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Hobbes cites the armed traveler, the door locked at night, and the chests locked at home, despite the laws and the armed public officers.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does the image of man as a wolf to man come from, according to the entry?
choix: From Plautus, cited by Hobbes in 1642 in the epistle of De Cive
From Hobbes, who invents it in Leviathan in 1651
From Cicero, whom Hobbes cites in chapter XIII of Leviathan
From Montaigne, in an essay from the late 16th century
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The wolf comes from Plautus; Hobbes cites it in De Cive alongside its opposite, man as a god to man among citizens.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does Hobbes see this condition of war at work, despite its general absence?
choix: Among merchants of the same town, who compete for customers
Between parents and children, within every family
Between sovereigns, who stand in the posture of gladiators, weapons pointed
Between judges and public officers, who are charged with punishing wrongs
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Hobbes cites the peoples of America without government, civil war, and sovereigns in the posture of gladiators, weapons pointed.
